Ten of the eleven heads with a dominant write are ordinary sink heads. Their top output direction lies mostly along the massive dimensions and the mean residual (cosine 0.55–0.99). L11h3 and L11h2, the heads that broadcast the end of the prompt, are at 0.99 and 0.97: they maintain the massive activations, nothing more.

The exception is **L22h0**, a late local-layer head. Its dominant output direction is unrelated to the mean residual (0.05), the massive dimensions (0.07), D1 (0.02) and the math contrast (0.08). It also has the lowest effective output rank of all 104 heads (54, against a typical 150–200). It sits four layers before the output and writes a strong, non-bookkeeping direction, so its write could act directly on next-token choice.

The next step is to build a difficulty-controlled contrast. Across passes 3, 5 and 9, many DEV problems received a correct answer from one model variant and a wrong one from another. Comparing the original model's internal states on those *matched* correct and wrong answers to the same problem removes the difficulty confound behind every correct-vs-failing contrast so far. If the difference concentrates in one direction that some specific component writes, that component would be a mechanistic lead. If it is diffuse, it confirms a distributed reasoning weakness.

From it I compute the matched correct-minus-wrong difference of answer-token means, per layer. The questions are whether that difference is consistent across two halves of the pairs and whether it is concentrated: a stable, low-dimensional direction that some identifiable head or neuron writes. A real failure mechanism would show as a consistent, concentrated difference tied to a component. A diffuse or inconsistent one means the errors are distributed reasoning slips, and I would then default to the original.
